This bill would merge several tribunals into one by changing the Administrative Appeals Tribunal Act.
It would set up a new governance structure, streamline procedures, and modernise the law, including new rules for divisions, appointments, and reviews.
The bill would also change how migration and refugee reviews are handled, with most of the usual rules not applying to them.
Provide a new objective for the combined tribunal.
Establish the tribunal's membership, including the President, Deputy Presidents, senior members, and others, with qualifications and conditions for appointment.
Set up divisions, assign members to them, and allow the President to make practice directions.
Introduce procedural rules for reviews, with special arrangements for migration and refugee cases.
Make minor changes to appeals to federal courts on legal questions.
Modernise machinery provisions, including offences and a new publication rule for decisions.
The amalgamated Tribunal, its members, and people involved in reviews before it, especially those in migration and refugee cases.

The Tribunals Amalgamation Bill merges the Administrative Appeals Tribunal, Migration Review Tribunal–Refugee Review Tribunal, and Social Security Appeals Tribunal into a single AAT, saving $7.2 million over the forward estimates. The Hon. Justice Duncan Kerr will remain as the first president of the amalgamated tribunal.

The speaker supported the Tribunals Amalgamation Bill 2015 to merge four Commonwealth tribunals into a single body, with Labor amendments preserving the AAT's independence, creating a specialist FOI division, and retaining seven-year member terms and removal by address of parliament. The speaker opposed the government's plan to abolish the Administrative Review Council and objected to a provision moving child support appeals from the Family Court to the Federal Court.

The speaker supported the Tribunals Amalgamation Bill 2015, arguing it simplifies merits review by merging key tribunals into the AAT, saving $7.2 million, and redirecting child support appeals from the Family Court to the Federal Court, as the Family Court hears only one or two such appeals annually.
